evidence.note: After the first NOA test passed, the agent hit 234 failing tests but never performed byte-diff analysis on its output vs goldens; it categorized failures by guesswork and moved to bulk implementation rather than tracing any diff to a root cause in the Java model.

Repeatedly acknowledged its layout algorithms 'just return sorted nodes instead of proper algorithm' and left them wrong; abandoned components (alignment/analysis left as stubs) rather than correcting the underlying model — matches anchor 0's 'abandons a component when the obvious fix fails.'

Did recognize 'we're going in circles with mass patching / blind regex replacement is causing more harm than good' and once resolved to fix files individually — a genuine course-correction, but about its own tooling workflow, not the Java-behavior model, and it relapsed into mass patching repeatedly.

The algorithmic understanding of link interleaving was inferred from golden files up front (reverse-engineering), not derived from correcting a falsified assumption via a byte-diff, so it doesn't count toward this dimension.

Trajectory ends still firefighting compilation errors from corrupted stubs (connected_components returning f64, etc.); no evidence of any diff-driven refinement of the Java format/algorithm model in the entire back half.

reasoning: The dimension asks whether the agent revised its model of Java behavior when a parity byte-diff falsified an assumption. The agent almost never reached that loop: it inferred the layout algorithm from goldens up front, passed a small set of basic tests, then abandoned the ~234 failing components as simplified stubs without ever diffing output against goldens or returning to the Java source to fix a general rule. Its only real course-correction was recognizing its destructive regex-patching workflow (adjacent tooling meta-work, and repeatedly relapsed), not a corrected Java-behavior model. This sits just above anchor 0 (forcing a failing approach / abandoning components) with a trace of self-awareness, well short of anchor 5's 're-read Java and adjust the approach' — placing it at 2.
